glossary:
  "Quarterback": "The offensive player who takes the snap on almost every play, hands the ball off or throws it, and usually relays the play call and makes the pre-snap adjustments."
  "Running back": {def: "The offensive back whose main job is to carry the ball on running plays; he also catches short passes and blocks blitzers. Lines up behind or beside the quarterback.", aliases: ["Halfback"]}
  "Fullback": "A bigger, blocking-first back who lines up in front of or beside the running back and leads him into the hole; now a rare, specialist position in the NFL."
  "Wide receiver": "A pass-catcher who lines up away from the linemen, near the sideline (split out wide) or in between (the slot). His main job is running routes and catching passes."
  "Tight end": "A hybrid of lineman and receiver who often lines up right next to a tackle (tight to the line), blocks on running plays and runs routes on passing plays."
  "Offensive line": "The five players in the middle of the offense (center, two guards, two tackles) who block on every play and may not catch forward passes."
  "Center": "The offensive lineman in the middle of the line who snaps the ball to the quarterback and then blocks; he usually also identifies which defender the blocking scheme counts from."
  "Guard": "One of the two offensive linemen on either side of the center."
  "Tackle (position)": "One of the two offensive linemen on the outside of the line, next to the guards; usually the tallest, longest-armed linemen, whose main job is blocking pass rushers off the edge."
  "Defensive tackle": "A defensive lineman who lines up inside, across from the guards or center, to clog the middle against the run and push the pocket on passes. In a four-man line one tackle usually absorbs double-teams over the center and the other (the 3-technique) shoots a gap and rushes the passer."
  "Nose tackle": "The defensive tackle lined up on (or nearly on) the center, usually the biggest player on the defense; in a three-man line, the middle lineman."
  "Defensive end": "A defensive lineman who lines up at or near the end of the defensive line, outside the offensive tackles; his main jobs are rushing the passer and keeping runs from getting outside."
  "Edge rusher": "The modern catch-all name for the defender whose main job is pressuring the quarterback from outside the offensive tackle, whether he's called a defensive end or an outside linebacker."
  "Linebacker": "A defender who lines up behind the defensive line (the second level) and does a bit of everything: tackling runners, covering short passes and sometimes rushing the passer."
  "Mike linebacker": "The middle linebacker (M), usually the defense's signal-caller, lined up in the middle of the formation."
  "Will linebacker": "The weak-side linebacker (W), lined up on the side of the formation away from the tight end; usually the fastest linebacker, who chases plays from behind."
  "Sam linebacker": "The strong-side linebacker (S), lined up on the tight end's side of the formation; usually the biggest linebacker, often the one taken off the field for a fifth defensive back."
  "Cornerback": "A defensive back who lines up across from the wide receivers, usually near the sideline, and covers them on passing plays."
  "Slot cornerback": {def: "A cornerback who covers the slot receiver, lining up inside between the outside corner and the linemen; the fifth defensive back in a nickel defense.", aliases: ["Nickel back"]}
  "Safety (position)": "A defensive back who lines up deepest, usually 10 to 15 yards off the ball, as the last line of defense against deep passes and long runs."
  "Free safety": "The safety who usually plays deeper and more in the middle of the field, 'free' to go wherever the ball goes rather than covering a particular receiver."
  "Strong safety": "The safety who usually lines up on the strong (tight end) side, a little closer to the line, and helps more against the run."
  "Kicker": "The specialist who kicks field goals, extra points and kickoffs."
  "Punter": "The specialist who punts the ball away on fourth down, standing about 15 yards behind the line."
  "Long snapper": "The specialist who snaps the ball the long distance back to the punter or holder on kicking plays."
  "Holder": "The player, usually the punter, who catches the long snap on a field goal or extra point and sets the ball on the ground for the kicker."
  "Returner": "The player on the receiving team who catches a kickoff or punt and tries to run it back."
  "Gunner": "On a punt, one of the two players split out wide who sprint downfield to tackle the returner; the other side assigns one or two blockers (vices) to slow each of them."
  "Eligible receiver": "An offensive player allowed to catch a forward pass: one of the two players on the ends of the line, or any back (anyone lined up off the line, behind it), except a quarterback taking the snap under center."
  "Ineligible receiver": "An offensive player who may not catch a forward pass: the interior linemen, anyone wearing 50-79 who hasn't reported as eligible, any player covered up inside the end of the line, and a quarterback taking the snap under center."
  "Skill positions": "The offense's ball-handling positions (quarterback, running back, wide receiver and tight end), as opposed to the linemen."
  "Front seven": "The defensive linemen and linebackers together, the defenders who line up near the ball and play the run first. (In a nickel defense it is often six, plus whoever fills the seventh spot.)"
  "Secondary": "The defensive backs as a group (cornerbacks and safeties), who line up farther from the ball and are responsible first for pass coverage."
  "Alignment": "Where a player lines up before the snap on a particular play: his spot, depth and position relative to the ball and to the other players."
  "Assignment": "A player's job on a particular play: whom he blocks, which route he runs, which gap he fills or which receiver or area he covers."

Sunday, a few minutes before kickoff. The broadcast cuts to a graphic: eleven faces, each
with a name, a college and two or three letters you only half recognize. *LT. RG. FS. Sam.*
Then the game starts and the announcer is talking faster than you can follow: "The nickel
is walking down over the slot... the Mike points at the Will... the tight end is the only
one in to block..." You know the quarterback. You can probably find the running back. And the
other twenty players on the field are, for most viewers, a blur of helmets. This chapter
fixes that. By the end, every one of those twenty-two people will have a name, a job and a
reason for existing, and you'll know the one distinction that makes the rest of the book
possible: the difference between who a player *is*, where he *stands* and what he's been
told to *do*.

**You'll be able to…**

- Name every offensive position (about eight names cover the eleven players) and say what
  each one does on a run and on a pass.
- Name the defensive positions, from the nose tackle to the free safety, and tell the Mike,
  Will and Sam linebackers apart by where the tight end lines up.
- Name the special-teams specialists (kicker, punter, long snapper, holder, returner, gunner)
  and find them on a field goal, a punt and a kickoff.
- Say which offensive players may legally catch a forward pass, and use jersey numbers to
  check.
- Explain why a guard and a cornerback have such different bodies, using real combine data.
- Separate a player's position from his alignment and his assignment, and explain why good
  coaches blur all three on purpose.

## Twenty-two players, three teams

At any moment eleven players per side are on the field. Not the same eleven, though. An NFL
team is really three teams that share a roster: an **offense** for when it has the ball, a
**defense** for when the other side has it, and a **special teams** unit for kicking plays
(kickoffs, punts, field goals and extra points, which you met in
[The Game in Fifteen Minutes](01-01-the-game-in-fifteen-minutes.qmd)). A team carries 53
players on its roster, and up to 48 of them dress for a game.[^roster] Between plays (never
during one) the coaches can swap in whoever they like, as often as they like; how the defense
gets the chance to answer the offense's substitutions is part of
[Personnel](../02-personnel-and-formations/02-01-personnel-groupings.qmd).

It wasn't always this way, and how it changed explains why NFL bodies look the way they do.
For football's first half-century most players played the whole game, offense *and*
defense, which meant every player had to be a compromise: big enough to block, quick enough
to cover, fit enough to last sixty minutes. Substitution rules were strict, so a player who
came out often couldn't go back in that quarter. The NFL loosened them during the Second
World War, when rosters were thin, and made **unlimited free substitution** permanent in
January 1950.[^platoon] Within a few years teams were using separate offensive and defensive
units ("two platoons"), and then specialists for kicking. The last great player who refused
to come off the field was the Eagles' Chuck Bednarik, a center on offense and a linebacker
on defense, who played almost all of the 1960 championship game and ended it by tackling the
Packers' Jim Taylor on the final play.[^bednarik] The modern exception proves how rare it is:
the Jaguars drafted Travis Hunter second overall in 2025 to play both receiver and cornerback,
and he took 326 offensive and 162 defensive snaps before a knee injury ended his rookie
season in late October.[^hunter]

Once a player only had to do one job, he could be built for that job. That is the single
biggest reason a modern roster contains 330-pound men who can't run a fast 40 (the 40-yard
dash, the sprint every prospect runs before the draft) and 190-pound men who can't block
anyone: each was chosen for a narrow, demanding task. We'll measure that with real data later
in the chapter.

### The whole picture first

Here are all twenty-two at once, in a traditional alignment. The offense is in a
**formation** (the way it arranges its players before the snap; formations get their own
chapters, starting with
[Formation Rules](../02-personnel-and-formations/02-02-formation-rules-and-vocabulary.qmd))
with two backs stacked behind the quarterback, against a classic "base" defense (four
linemen, three linebackers, four defensive backs). You'll rarely see this exact picture on a
modern Sunday (we'll see the more common one shortly), but it's the clearest way to meet
every position, because each one is in its classic spot.

**How to read the field diagrams in this book.** The offense moves up the page. The blue
line across the field is the line of scrimmage, the imaginary line through the ball that
neither side may cross before the snap (defined fully in
[Downs, Distance, and Field Position](01-02-downs-distance-and-field-position.qmd)); the thick
yellow-orange line is the line to gain, ten yards ahead here. Offensive players are blue
circles, defenders are orange squares, and each wears a short tag. Offense: **Q**
quarterback, **R** running back, **F** fullback, **X**, **Z** and **H** wide receivers, **Y**
(and sometimes **U**) tight ends, and **LT LG C RG RT** the offensive linemen from left to
right (diagrams often leave the linemen's tags off). Defense: **E** defensive end, **T**
defensive tackle, **N** nose tackle, **S M W** the Sam, Mike and Will linebackers, **CB**
cornerback, **$** the slot cornerback, **FS** and **SS** the free and strong safeties. Shape
and color always tell the sides apart, so a blue **C** (center) is never an orange **CB**. A
colored ring marks a player to watch.

Take a moment with that picture before we go player by player. A few patterns are already
visible:

- **The middle is crowded and heavy; the edges are open and light.** Ten big men (five
  offensive linemen, four defensive linemen, plus a tight end) are packed into about twelve
  yards of width around the ball. The fastest, lightest players (receivers and cornerbacks)
  are out near the sidelines.
- **The offense is lined up in rows by depth.** Seven players on the line of scrimmage, then
  the backs behind. That's not a style choice; it's a rule, and it decides who can catch a
  pass. We'll get to it.
- **The defense is lined up in layers.** Linemen within a yard of the ball, linebackers four
  or five yards back, cornerbacks out wide about seven yards off, safeties deepest of all. The
  closer a defender is to the ball, the more he's built to stop the run; the farther away, the
  more he's built to stop the pass.

## The offensive line: five men who never touch the ball

Start in the middle, because every play does. The [**offensive line**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-offensive-line)
is the five players shoulder-to-shoulder around the ball: a center, two guards and two
tackles. On every snap, run or pass, their job is to block. They almost never touch the ball
(the center touches it once, at the snap), they're almost never mentioned on the broadcast
unless something goes wrong, and they decide more games than anyone except the quarterback.

From the inside out:

- The [**center**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-center) (**C**) is in the middle. He
  starts every play with the [**snap**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-snap), handing or
  tossing the ball back between his legs, and then becomes a blocker like the others, often
  against the biggest defender on the field, with his head still coming up from the snap.
  Before the snap he's usually the line's communicator: he points at one linebacker and
  calls him the "Mike" for this play, and every lineman counts from that man to work out whom
  he blocks. That call, the [**Mike ID**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-mike-id), is
  explained in [Pass Protection](../04-the-passing-game/04-02-pass-protection.qmd).
- The two [**guards**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-guard) (**LG**, **RG**) line up on
  either side of the center. They are often the most powerful linemen, built for short,
  violent collisions with defensive tackles in a phone booth of space. On some runs a guard
  [**pulls**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-pull): he opens his hips at the snap and runs
  along the line, just behind it, to block on the other side, which is why guards tend to be
  a bit quicker than you'd expect.
- The two [**tackles**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-tackle-position) (**LT**, **RT**)
  are on the outside of the line. Tackles are usually the tallest linemen with the longest
  arms, because their hardest job is pass protection against the fastest defenders on the
  field: speed rushers coming from outside, running a wide arc toward the quarterback. A
  tackle has to slide backward and sideways fast enough to stay in front of a man fifty
  pounds lighter.

**Why so big?** Because blocking is mostly physics. A blocker's job is to move a defender
off a spot, or to keep the defender from moving him off his, and mass and leverage win
those contests. Offensive linemen at the NFL Scouting Combine (the league's annual
pre-draft testing event) average a little over 310 pounds and about 6-foot-5.[^combine] What
they give up is speed: a typical lineman runs the 40 in a bit over 5.2 seconds, which is very
fast for a 310-pound person and slower than nearly everyone else on the field.

::: {.callout-caution title="Common misconception: the left tackle is always the best lineman"}
For decades the left tackle was the glamour job on the line, and for a good reason. Most
quarterbacks are right-handed, so when they set up to throw they face right and their back
is to the left: the **blind side**. Michael Lewis built *The Blind Side* (2006) around this,
opening with Lawrence Taylor's 1985 sack that broke Joe Theismann's leg and tracing how that
kind of threat drove left-tackle salaries up.[^blindside]

That logic still exists, but it's weaker than it was. Modern defenses move their best pass
rusher to whichever side they like, often snap to snap; left-handed quarterbacks flip the
whole thing; and the right tackle usually faces more run-blocking in front of the tight end.
The best tackle in football can play on the right. The Lions drafted **Penei Sewell**
seventh overall in 2021, played him at right tackle, and in April 2024 made him, at the
time, the highest-paid offensive lineman in the NFL on a four-year, $112 million
extension. For 2026, after their long-time left tackle Taylor Decker left, they moved Sewell
to the left side,[^sewell] which tells you both halves of the story: the best tackle doesn't
*have* to play on the left, but when a team has to choose, the blind side still pulls. Judge
a lineman by how often you *don't* hear about him.
:::

The offensive line has one more defining feature, the one that matters most to you as a
viewer: **these five may not catch a forward pass** (more on that soon). And they wear
numbers in the 50s, 60s and 70s, so you can always find them.

## The quarterback

The [**quarterback**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-quarterback) (**Q**) lines up
directly behind the center, either with his hands under the center's backside to take a
hand-to-hand snap ([**under center**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-under-center)) or
standing about five yards back to take a short toss (the
[**shotgun**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-shotgun)). He touches the ball on almost
every offensive play: he hands it off, fakes a handoff, throws it, or runs with it.

You know the quarterback already, so here's what you might not. His most important work
often happens *before* the snap. He usually receives the play call through the radio in his
helmet and repeats it to the others ([What a Play Really Is](01-04-what-a-play-really-is.qmd)).
At the line he reads the defense and may change the protection or the whole play. After
the snap, on a pass, he isn't just "finding the open man": he's working through a planned
order of receivers, the [**progression**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-progression)
([Passing Game Fundamentals](../04-the-passing-game/04-01-passing-fundamentals.qmd)), while
three-hundred-pound men close in, usually releasing the ball in under three seconds. That's
why quarterbacks are the most expensive players in the sport, and why the body type is the
least uniform on the field: from 5-foot-10 scramblers to 6-foot-6 pocket passers, what makes
a quarterback is mostly invisible (processing speed, accuracy, nerve).

## The backs: running back and fullback

Behind (or beside) the quarterback are the **backs**. The names are fossils, inherited from
rugby, where the backs stood in rows by depth: quarter-backs nearest the scrimmage, half-backs
behind them, a full-back deepest. (You'll often read that the fractions measured literal
distances, a quarter, half or all of the way back. That's too neat; the fractions worked more
like "first, second and last row.")[^backs] The formations changed and the names stuck,
which is why today's fullback lines up *in front of* today's halfback.

Keep one more meaning of "back" in your pocket, because the rulebook uses it: **any offensive
player who isn't on the line of scrimmage at the snap is a back**, whatever his position. A
wide receiver standing a yard off the line is, legally, a back. That turns out to decide who
may catch a pass.

The [**running back**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-running-back) (**R**; often called
the tailback when he's the deepest back), also called the
[**halfback**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-halfback), is the offense's main ball
carrier on running plays. Most offenses use one at a time. He takes handoffs and finds the
hole (the opening his blockers make; coaches call the spaces between linemen **gaps** and
give them letters, as [The Language of the Run Game](../03-the-run-game/03-01-run-game-language.qmd)
shows), catches short passes (often as the last option, the "checkdown"), and on passing
plays he frequently stays in to block a blitzing linebacker (one who rushes the quarterback
instead of dropping into coverage) before slipping out. Running backs are among the shortest
players on the field but heavy for their height: low center of gravity, thick legs, hard to
knock over, quick enough to make a defender miss in a small space.

The [**fullback**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-fullback) (**F**) is a bigger back,
built to block. In the classic two-back offense he lines up between the quarterback and the
tailback and leads into the hole ahead of the runner, hitting the first linebacker who shows
up. He carries the ball occasionally (often on short-yardage plunges) and catches the odd
pass.

You see fewer fullbacks than your parents did. As offenses spread out with three and four
receivers, the second back was the obvious player to remove, and many NFL teams now carry no
true fullback at all. The ones who remain tend to be unusually versatile, because a player
who can only lead-block is hard to justify on a 53-man roster.

::: {.callout-note title="Film room: 49ers 2017–2025 — the fullback who outlived his position"}
**Kyle Juszczyk** signed with San Francisco in 2017, when Kyle Shanahan became head coach,
and was still there in 2026, his tenth season with the team: a Harvard graduate the Ravens
had drafted in the fourth round in 2013, paid like a starter at a position most teams had
stopped starting. By the end of the 2025 season he'd been picked for ten straight Pro Bowls,
the most ever by a fullback.[^juszczyk]

Why keep a fullback in the age of the spread? Because Shanahan's offense is built on the
run game and on making the defense guess, and Juszczyk lets one set of eleven players line
up in many different formations. In the same game he lines up as a lead-blocking fullback, as
a tight end on the line, as a [**wing**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-wing) (a yard off
the line just outside the tight end), or split out like a receiver, and he catches passes
from all of them. The defense sees two backs on the field and has to keep its bigger,
run-stopping players out there, and then the 49ers throw.

## Wide receivers: X, Z and the slot

The [**wide receivers**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-wide-receiver) are the offense's
specialist pass-catchers, lined up away from the linemen: "split out" wide near the
sideline, or in between, in the area called the [**slot**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-slot).
Their job on a pass is to run a **route** (a planned path, with timing, that you'll learn to
read in [Passing Game Fundamentals](../04-the-passing-game/04-01-passing-fundamentals.qmd)), get
open and catch the ball. On a run, they block the defensive backs downfield, a thankless job
that turns eight-yard runs into forty-yard ones.

Coaches give each receiver spot a letter, and you'll hear them on broadcasts:

- The **X** receiver lines up on the line of scrimmage, usually on the side away from the
  tight end. Someone has to: the rules (coming up) want seven players on the line, and on the
  side without a tight end, X is the end of it. That costs him twice. Only a player *off* the
  line may be moving at the snap, so X can't go in
  [**motion**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-motion) (running across the formation before
  the snap; see [The Pre-Snap Phase](01-05-the-pre-snap-phase.qmd)), and with no cushion and
  no running start he's the easiest receiver to jam at the line. So the X is often the team's
  strongest outside receiver, the one who can beat that contact on his own.
- The **Z** receiver lines up a yard *off* the line, usually on the tight end's side. Being
  off the ball keeps the tight end at the end of the line, and so still eligible (you'll see why
  that matters in a moment), gives Z a little room against a jam, and makes him the receiver
  most often sent in motion.
- The **slot** receiver (often called **H**) lines up between the outside receiver and the
  linemen, usually off the line. Slot receivers work in the middle of the field against
  linebackers and safeties, so they tend to be quick, sure-handed and good at getting open
  quickly in traffic rather than outrunning a cornerback over forty yards.

Treat the letters as a dialect, not a law. In some offenses Y is a slot receiver rather than a
tight end, F is the fullback in one system and the slot in another, U is often a second tight
end, and many teams flip X and Z by formation. **The letter names a spot, not a person**,
which is this chapter's big idea in miniature. The full vocabulary, and the older names
(split end for X, flanker for Z), belong to
[Formation Rules and the Language of Alignment](../02-personnel-and-formations/02-02-formation-rules-and-vocabulary.qmd).

Receivers are the closest thing football has to sprinters: around 6-foot-1 and 200 pounds
on average, with a typical combine 40 of about 4.5 seconds.

## The tight end: half lineman, half receiver

The [**tight end**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-tight-end) (**Y**) is the most
interesting position on the offense, because he's two positions at once. In the classic
alignment he lines up on the line of scrimmage right next to a tackle, "tight" to the line,
as opposed to a split end out wide. From there he can do either of two very different
jobs: block a defensive end or linebacker like a sixth lineman, or release into a route like
a receiver.

That's exactly why he matters to the defense. When a wide receiver comes on the field, the
defense can count on a pass threat; when an extra lineman comes on, it can count on a run.
A tight end who can do both forces the defense to defend both. Bodies show it: tight ends
average about 6-foot-4 and 250 pounds, between a lineman and a receiver, and run a 40 in about
4.7 seconds: slower than a receiver, and about as fast as the linebackers who usually cover
him. His edge over a linebacker isn't speed. It's that he's a trained route runner with a
receiver's hands and a bigger catch radius, against a run defender trying to cover.

The side the tight end lines up on is so important that it has a name, the
[**strong side**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-strong-side) of the formation (the other is
the weak side). As you'll see in a moment, several defensive positions are *named* for which
side of the tight end they line up on.

**Travis Kelce** of the Chiefs, a third-round pick in 2013, is the tight end of his era. He
had seven straight 1,000-yard receiving seasons from 2016 to 2022, a record for a tight end
(no other tight end had more than four 1,000-yard seasons at the time).[^kelce] Watch him and
you'll see the position's whole point: on one snap he's in-line blocking a defensive end,
on the next he's split out alone, and the defense has to decide who covers a 255-pounder
who runs routes like a receiver.

His older brother, **Jason Kelce**, was the Eagles' center from 2011 to 2023, which makes
the Kelces a nice demonstration of this chapter's theme: two brothers, one family's genes,
two completely different jobs. At the combine Travis weighed 255 pounds and Jason, an
undersized center, 280. In Super Bowl LVII (February 2023) they played against each other:
the Chiefs beat the Eagles 38–35.[^sblvii]

## Skill positions, eligible receivers and who may catch a pass

Football broadcasters and fantasy players talk about the [**skill positions**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-skill-positions):
quarterback, running back, wide receiver and tight end, the players who handle the ball. (It's
a slightly insulting name, as any offensive lineman will tell you, because blocking is a
skill too.) The skill positions overlap closely with a rule that matters a great deal to
the strategy of the game: not everyone on the offense is allowed to catch a forward pass.

The rules start with how the offense must line up:[^eligible]

1. **At least seven players must be on the line of scrimmage** at the snap. So at most four
   are off it, in the backfield.
2. Of the players on the line, **only the two on the ends** are
   [**eligible receivers**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-eligible-receiver), allowed to
   catch a forward pass.
3. **Every back is eligible**, and remember what "back" means here: anyone lined up off the
   line, whether he's a running back, a receiver a yard off the ball or the quarterback.
   There is one exception: a quarterback who takes the snap hand-to-hand under center. A
   quarterback in the shotgun is just another back and may catch a pass. The Eagles won
   Super Bowl LII (February 2018) partly on that rule: on fourth-and-goal, quarterback Nick
   Foles walked up behind his right tackle as if changing the call, the snap went straight to
   the running back, and tight end Trey Burton threw it to the uncovered Foles for a
   touchdown, the "Philly Special."[^philly]
4. Everyone else is an [**ineligible receiver**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-ineligible-receiver):
   the interior linemen, any player covered up inside the end of the line, and anyone wearing
   a number from 50 to 79 who hasn't told the referee before the play that he's reporting as
   eligible.

Notice something about that picture: the X receiver and the tight end are on the line, and
the Z and the slot receiver are a yard behind it. Those one-yard differences aren't style.
Every receiver's spot is a choice about who is on the line, and so who is eligible. If the
Z had stepped up onto the line outside the tight end, the tight end would no longer be at
the end of the line; he'd be "covered," and ineligible on that play. Offenses use that on
purpose, and officials watch for it. (Formation Rules works through covered receivers,
tackles who report as eligible, and the trick formations built on both.)

A related rule you'll hear about on run-pass plays: ineligible linemen may not go more than
one yard downfield before a forward pass is thrown. That rule, and why it shapes modern
offenses, is in [Run-Pass Options](../04-the-passing-game/04-06-rpos.qmd).

::: {.callout-important title="Why it exists: eligibility"}
The line-up rule came first, and its target wasn't the pass. When college football rewrote
its rules in 1910, after years of deaths and injuries, it required seven offensive players on
the line of scrimmage, to stop the "mass plays" in which a whole team built a moving wedge
around the ball carrier: with only four men behind the line, as the rule-makers put it, "the
weight of attack is necessarily reduced."[^seven]

Once seven men had to stand on the line, the rules had to say which of them could catch
the newly legal forward pass, and the answer (the two ends and the backs) gives the game its
balance. The five interior men become pure blockers, so the offense can't flood the field
with receivers; and because eligibility is announced by where players *stand*, the defense
can see who might get the ball before the snap. That's why the line-up rules are so fussy:
a one-yard step changes who can catch the ball.
:::

The system loosened twice recently. In 2021, owners approved a Kansas City proposal letting
running backs, receivers, tight ends, linebackers and defensive backs wear single digits

## The defense: front seven and secondary

Now turn around. The defense is easiest to understand as two groups, which you saw bracketed
in the first diagram:

- The [**front seven**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-front-seven): the defensive linemen
  and the linebackers, the defenders who line up near the ball and play the run first.
- The [**secondary**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-secondary): the cornerbacks and
  safeties, the "defensive backs," who line up farther away and are responsible first for
  the pass.

That split is a trade-off the defense makes on every play. Defenders near the ball are
quick to the runner but poorly placed to cover a receiver thirty yards downfield; defenders
far away are the reverse. A coordinator's most basic decision is how many to put in the
[**box**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-box) (the area around the ball where runs are
fought: from just outside one end of the offensive line to just outside the other, and about
five to seven yards deep) and how many to keep back. The number standing in the box at the
snap is the [**box count**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-box-count), which
[A First Look at Defense](../02-personnel-and-formations/02-05-a-first-look-at-defense.qmd)
teaches you to take.

### Defensive line: tackles, the nose and ends

The defensive linemen line up within a yard or so of the ball, in a three- or four-point
stance (one or two hands on the ground), across from the offensive linemen. Their job is the
mirror image of the offensive line's: on runs, hold their ground, fill their
[**gap**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-gap-a-b-c-d) (the space between two offensive
linemen that the defense assigns them), and shed blocks to make tackles; on passes, get to
the quarterback.

- The [**defensive tackles**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-defensive-tackle) (**T**)
  line up inside, across from the guards and center. They are the heaviest defenders, and in
  a four-man line the two of them usually split the work. One lines up shaded on the center
  and is built to absorb blockers, often two at once, so the linebackers behind him can run
  free. The other, the [**3-technique**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-3-technique), lines
  up on a guard's outside shoulder and is built to shoot through a gap and rush the passer;
  he is usually the more valuable of the two. Either way, a good one collapses the
  [**pocket**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-pocket) (the protected space the blockers form
  around the quarterback) from the inside, which is worse for a quarterback than pressure from
  the outside: his escape from an edge rusher is to step *forward*, and an inside rush takes
  that away.
- The [**nose tackle**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-nose-tackle) (**N**) is the
  defensive tackle who lines up on (or nearly on) the center. In a defense with three linemen
  he's the one in the middle, directly across from the center, and he's usually the biggest
  man on the defense. The Eagles' **Jordan Davis**, a nose tackle drafted in 2022, measured
  6-foot-6 and 341 pounds at the combine and then ran the 40 in 4.78 seconds, as fast as the
  typical quarterback.[^combine2]
- The [**defensive ends**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-defensive-end) (**E**) line up on
  the outside, across from or outside the offensive tackles. They're lighter and faster than
  tackles, because their two jobs both happen in open space: rush the passer around the edge,
  and on runs, keep the ball carrier from getting outside them.

Where exactly each lineman stands has its own vocabulary. A lineman is
[**head-up**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-head-up) when he's directly across from a
blocker and [**shaded**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-shade) when he's offset onto one of
the blocker's shoulders, and coaches number those spots as
[**techniques**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-technique-alignment-number) ("the 3" is the
guard's outside shoulder; "the 1" is a shade on the center).
[The Language of the Run Game](../03-the-run-game/03-01-run-game-language.qmd) introduces the
numbers and
[Defensive Line Play](../05-defensive-fronts-and-run-defense/05-01-dl-techniques-and-gap-control.qmd)
deepens them.

**Aaron Donald**, who played for the Rams from 2014 until he retired after the 2023 season,
is the archetype of a defensive tackle who broke the mold. At 6-foot-1 and about 285 pounds
he was an undersized 3-technique, and teams worried about it before the draft. Then he ran a
4.68 40 at the combine, a time you'd expect from a linebacker. He became the most disruptive
interior lineman of his era, three times Defensive Player of the Year.[^donald] He's useful to
remember for a simple reason: he shows what the "size" norms in this chapter are for. They're
not rules, they're the average solutions to a physics problem, and a player who solves the
problem differently (with quickness instead of mass) can be better than all of them.

### Edge rushers

The [**edge rusher**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-edge-rusher) is the modern name for
the defender whose main job is getting to the quarterback from outside the offensive tackle.
You'll hear "edge" constantly now, and the reason is that the old position names stopped
fitting. A [**4-3**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-4-3) defense (four linemen, three
linebackers, the one in our first picture) calls its edge rushers defensive ends, and they
usually put a hand on the ground. A [**3-4**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-3-4) defense
(three linemen, *four* linebackers) uses its two *outside* linebackers as the edge rushers,
usually standing up, and its two *inside* linebackers split the Mike's job between them. Same
job, two names, so the league's vocabulary converged on "edge." Even the Scouting Combine
created an "EDGE" workout group in 2018 instead of choosing between DE and OLB.[^combine3]

Edge rushers are among the most valuable players in football, because pass pressure wrecks
offenses and the edge is where most of it comes from. **T.J. Watt** of the Steelers is
the model: technically an outside linebacker in a 3-4, 6-foot-4 and 252 pounds at his
combine, he tied the single-season sack record with 22.5 in 2021, and that record stood until
Myles Garrett, a 4-3 defensive end in Cleveland, got to 23 in 2025.[^sacks] How edge rushers
win (and why "pressures" matter more than sacks) is the subject of
[The Pass Rush](../07-pressure/07-01-pass-rush.qmd).

### Linebackers: Mike, Will and Sam

The [**linebackers**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-linebacker) line up behind the
defensive line, usually four or five yards off the ball: the "second level" of the defense.
They are the defense's all-purpose players. On a run, they read the play and fill the gap
the runner is heading for; on a pass, they drop into coverage on the short middle of the
field or cover a back or tight end; and sometimes they
[**blitz**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-blitz), rushing the quarterback themselves. Their
bodies are a compromise between the size to take on a fullback and the speed to cover a
running back.

In a defense with three linebackers, each has a one-letter name, and the classic rule is that
the letters come from where they line up *relative to the offense's tight end*:

- The [**Mike linebacker**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-mike-linebacker) (**M**) is the
  middle linebacker. He's usually the defense's signal-caller, often the one with the radio in
  his helmet (the "green dot," which [What a Play Really Is](01-04-what-a-play-really-is.qmd)
  explains), and he's the player you see pointing and shouting adjustments before the snap.
  The 49ers' **Fred Warner**, a third-round pick in 2018, is the modern ideal: a Mike who runs
  and covers like a safety.
- The [**Sam linebacker**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-sam-linebacker) (**S**) is the
  *strong-side* linebacker: he lines up on the tight end's side, and if the tight end moves to
  the other side before the snap, the Sam goes with him. He's usually the biggest and most
  physical of the three, because he has to take on a tight end's block. He's also usually the
  first linebacker to leave the field when the offense spreads out, as you'll see in a moment.
- The [**Will linebacker**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-will-linebacker) (**W**) is the
  *weak-side* linebacker, away from the tight end. With fewer blockers on his side, he's often
  the hardest linebacker for the offense to reach: someone has to climb off the line or come
  from the backfield to get to him, and plays to his side often have to account for him
  specially. So the Will tends to be the fastest of the three, a chaser who runs plays down
  from behind.

What if there's no tight end, or two? Then the defense needs another rule for "strong," and
teams differ: the side with more receivers (the passing strength), the wide side of the
field, or the side the running back is on. Often the Mike simply *declares* the strength with
a call before the snap, and everyone, the strong safety included, sets to it.
[Formation Rules](../02-personnel-and-formations/02-02-formation-rules-and-vocabulary.qmd)
lays out the options as [**formation strength**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-formation-strength);
for now, the tight end rule gets you through most first-and-10 snaps.

These letters are a dialect too: a 3-4 team may call its weak-side edge the "Jack" and its
second inside linebacker the "Mo," a slot defender may be the "Star," and a sixth defensive
back the "Money" (this book's **$** tag for the slot corner is the same pun). Linebackers'
reads and keys are the subject of
[Linebackers](../05-defensive-fronts-and-run-defense/05-04-linebackers-and-second-level.qmd).

::: {.callout-note title="Madden vs. real life"}
In a video game, a position is a slot on a depth chart: put a player at "LB" and the game
stands him where linebackers go, every snap. Real defenses name *spots*, and then decide how
players fill them. Some keep the same player at Sam and flip him to the strength wherever it
is. Others play **field and boundary**: one linebacker always takes the wide side of the
field and another the short side, so a player stays put while his letter changes with the
formation. Either way, learn the positions as jobs defined relative to the offense, not as
fixed spots on your screen.
:::

### The secondary: cornerbacks, the slot corner and safeties

The defensive backs are the lightest, fastest players on the defense, and the ones who
stand between a receiver and the end zone.

- The [**cornerbacks**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-cornerback) (**CB**) line up across
  from the outside wide receivers, near the sidelines, anywhere from right in the receiver's
  face ("press") to eight or nine yards off. Their job is pass coverage, either following a
  receiver wherever he goes ([**man coverage**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-man-coverage))
  or guarding an area of the field ([**zone**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-zone-coverage)).
  Corners are smaller than receivers on average and just as fast: the typical combine 40 is
  about 4.5 seconds, tied with receivers for the fastest on the field. The hardest thing in
  their job is that they must react: the receiver knows where he's going and the corner has
  to mirror him running backward or sideways.
- The [**slot cornerback**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-slot-cornerback) (**$**), also
  called the [**nickel back**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-nickel-back), covers the slot
  receiver. He lines up inside, between the outside cornerback and the box, so he's part
  cornerback and part linebacker: he has to cover quick receivers in the middle of the field
  *and* tackle runners and blitz off the edge. We'll see where he comes from below.
- The [**safeties**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-safety-position) line up deepest,
  usually 10 to 15 yards off the ball: the last line of defense against long passes and
  long runs. Most defenses have two:
  - the [**free safety**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-free-safety) (**FS**), who
    usually plays deeper and in the middle, "free" of responsibility for a particular
    receiver so that he can go wherever the ball goes; and
  - the [**strong safety**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-strong-safety) (**SS**), who
    lines up on the strong side, often a bit closer to the line, and helps more against the
    run.

How many safeties stay deep before the snap (one or two) is the most important single clue
you'll learn to read on defense. [A First Look at Defense](../02-personnel-and-formations/02-05-a-first-look-at-defense.qmd)
starts that habit, and [Coverage Fundamentals](../06-pass-coverage/06-01-coverage-fundamentals.qmd)
builds it out.

Two substitutions happened there, one on each side, and they're connected. The offense took
off its fullback and put on a third receiver. If the defense stayed in its base personnel,
somebody would have to line up over that receiver in the slot, and the only candidates are
linebackers: a 235-pound run defender against a quick, 190-pound receiver in open space, a
matchup offenses hunt for. So the defense takes off a linebacker and puts on a fifth
defensive back, the slot corner, who can run with him wherever the slot is. The linebacker who
leaves is usually the Sam, the biggest and least coverage-minded of the three, *even when the
slot is on the other side*: the remaining two shift over, and the slot corner goes to the slot.
Notice the picture also keeps a defender outside the tight end. With the Sam gone, the
defensive end slides out over him, so a run around the right end still has someone to beat.

That fifth defensive back has a name you'll hear in every broadcast: the defense is in
[**nickel**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-nickel) (five defensive backs: a nickel is
five cents). On obvious passing downs some defenses go further and play a sixth defensive
back, [**dime**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-dime) (two nickels). The offensive grouping
has a name too: one back and one tight end is
[**11 personnel**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-11-personnel). Both systems of shorthand
get full chapters: [Personnel](../02-personnel-and-formations/02-01-personnel-groupings.qmd)
for the offense's numbers and A First Look at Defense for the defense's packages ("base,"
nickel, dime).

How common is this picture? In 2025, about three NFL plays in five had exactly one back and
one tight end on the field, by far the most common grouping,[^personnel] and defenses were in
their "base" package (with three linebackers) on under 30% of plays.[^base] In practical
terms the slot cornerback is a starter on every defense, even though he isn't one of the
eleven on the "base" diagram. Not every fifth defensive back is a cornerback, though: some
defenses use a third *safety* instead, a bigger player who can also fit against the run (the
[**big nickel**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-big-nickel)).

Notice also what the defense calls its front now: four linemen and two linebackers make six,
not seven. "Front seven" is a habit of language from the base-defense era. In nickel, the
seventh man in the front on run downs is whoever the defense brings near the ball, and the
choice tells you what it fears. A safety walking down into the box before the snap says
"we expect a run, and we'll pay for it in pass coverage"; both safeties staying deep with only
six in the box says "pass first, and we dare you to run."

- The [**kicker**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-kicker) (**K**) kicks field goals, extra
  points and (on most teams) kickoffs. NFL kickers are specialists in the purest sense: they
  practice one motion and are judged on it in front of 70,000 people.
- The [**punter**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-punter) (**P**) punts the ball away on
  fourth down, standing about 15 yards behind the line so that rushers can't reach him before
  he kicks. Punters are judged on distance *and* hang time (how long the ball stays in the
  air), because hang time gives the coverage team time to get downfield.
- The [**long snapper**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-long-snapper) (**LS**) snaps the
  ball on punts, field goals and extra points. Why not just use the starting center? Because
  it's a different skill. A center hands the ball up or tosses it five yards to a quarterback
  who's waiting for it; a long snapper, head down and looking backward between his legs, has
  to fire a tight spiral seven yards to a holder or fifteen to a punter in well under a
  second, with the laces landing where they should, and then block. On a field goal, the snap,
  the hold and the kick together are drilled to take about 1.3 seconds.[^optime] A bad snap is
  the most catastrophic error in the kicking game, which is why every team keeps a dedicated
  one, and the rules protect him: on a punt or kick, no defender within a yard of the line may
  line up directly over the snapper.[^snapper]
- The [**holder**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-holder) catches the snap on a field goal
  or extra point and sets the ball on its point for the kicker. On most NFL teams the holder
  is the punter: he has the best hands for a long snap among the specialists, and he's on the
  field anyway.
- The [**returner**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-returner) catches kickoffs and punts and
  tries to run them back. Returners are usually fast backs, receivers or defensive backs.
- The [**gunner**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-gunner) is the punt team's missile: one
  of two players split out wide whose only job is to sprint downfield and tackle the
  returner. The return team answers by putting one or two blockers on each gunner, called
  **vices** or jammers, to hold him up at the line
  ([Field Goals, Extra Points, and the Punting Game](../09-special-teams-and-the-rules-that-shape-strategy/09-01-kicking-and-punting.qmd)

rules were tweaked again for 2025 and 2026, so they get their own chapter,
[Kickoffs, Returns, and the Dynamic Kickoff](../09-special-teams-and-the-rules-that-shape-strategy/09-02-kickoffs-and-returns.qmd).

Read the top panel from left to right and it sorts the field into families:

- **The speed family** (left, 190–215 lb): cornerbacks, wide receivers, safeties, running
  backs, and, interestingly, kickers, who are built like defensive backs.
- **The hybrids** (middle, 220–265 lb): quarterbacks, linebackers, fullbacks, tight ends and
  edge rushers, plus the long snappers. These are the positions whose jobs mix contact with
  space: a linebacker has to take on a fullback *and* cover a back; a tight end has to block
  an end *and* get open against a linebacker.
- **The big men** (right, 300+ lb): offensive linemen and defensive tackles, almost
  indistinguishable from each other in size, because they spend every snap pushing against
  each other.

The bottom panel shows the price of mass: weight and 40 time fall along nearly a straight
line (dashed). Each extra 20 pounds costs roughly a tenth of a second over 40 yards, and the
positions sit along that line wherever their job puts the balance between force and
speed. Edge rushers sit a little above the line (fast for their size), which is why they're
so hard to block; Aaron Donald sits *far* above it, about three-tenths of a second faster than
a typical 285-pounder, which is why he was Aaron Donald.

**Why does this matter to a viewer?** Because body type is how you'll recognize positions
when the alignment is ambiguous, and how you'll spot the mismatches offenses and defenses
hunt for. A 250-pound tight end covered by a 190-pound cornerback is a mismatch in one
direction (the tight end can shield the ball with his body); the same tight end covered by a
240-pound linebacker is a mismatch in the other (the tight end runs routes and catches like a
receiver; the linebacker is a run defender trying to cover). Half of play-calling is creating
one of those pictures and the other half is avoiding them. And the size bands explain one of
the oldest jokes in football analysis: "he's a tweener," a player whose body sits between two
families and doesn't clearly fit either job. Some tweeners never find a role; others (Kyle
Hamilton, below) become the most valuable players on their team because they can do both
jobs.

How much each position is *worth*, in salary and draft picks, is a separate and fascinating
question for [Building a Roster](../14-the-business-of-scheme/14-01-building-a-roster.qmd).

## Position, alignment, assignment

Everything so far has treated a position as if it told you what a player does. It doesn't,
quite. To read a play, you have to separate three different things:

- **Position** is who the player *is*: what the roster says, what he's built for, which
  meeting room he sits in during the week. Kyle Hamilton is a safety.
- [**Alignment**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-alignment) is where he *lines up* on this
  play: his spot, depth and relation to the ball and the other players. Hamilton might be
  12 yards deep, over the slot receiver, or standing in the box beside the linebackers.
- [**Assignment**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-assignment) is what he's been told to
  *do* on this play: which gap he fills, which receiver or area he covers, whether he rushes.
  From any of those alignments, Hamilton might blitz, cover the tight end man-to-man, or
  drop into a deep half of the field.

Why does the difference matter? Because **football is a game of disguise and recognition**,
and the gap between these three is where the disguise lives. A defense that lines a safety
up deep and *then* sends him on a blitz has used alignment to hide assignment. An offense
that lines its running back up as a wide receiver is forcing the defense to decide: do we
cover him with a linebacker (who's good against running backs) or a cornerback (who's good
against receivers)? Everything in this book about reading the game comes down to using
alignment to guess assignment before the snap, and then checking yourself after it.

It's also why rosters are more fluid than position labels suggest:

- The 49ers' **Deebo Samuel**, a wide receiver, was lined up in the backfield and handed the
  ball so often in 2021 that he called himself a "wide back"; his eight rushing touchdowns
  that season were the most by a receiver since 1970.[^deebo]
- Juszczyk, the film-room fullback, spends much of his time lined up as a tight end or a
  receiver.
- Many defenses play a safety at linebacker on passing downs, list their best edge rusher as
  a "linebacker," or use a "safety" who plays almost every down near the line, and teams
  increasingly don't care what the roster calls him.

Even the official data struggles with this: the participation data behind the two-backs
chart lists each player by his *roster* position, so it records who's on the field, not where
he stood.

::: {.callout-note title="Film room: Ravens 2022–2025 — Kyle Hamilton, one position, every alignment"}
The Ravens drafted **Kyle Hamilton** 14th overall in 2022.[^hamilton] He's a safety, and an
unusual one: 6-foot-4 and 220 pounds at his combine, a height only about one safety in forty
measured there since 2010 has matched, built more like a big receiver or a small linebacker.
Some evaluators worried about where he'd fit.

Baltimore's answer was: everywhere. Watch the Ravens' defense and find number 14 before
every snap. On one play he's a deep safety; on the next he's lined up over the slot like a
nickel back (when he does, the Ravens are playing a big nickel); on the next he's in the box
beside the linebackers, or walked up on the line over a tight end. He blitzes, covers tight
ends man-to-man, and plays deep zones, so an offense can't tell from his position what he's
about to do, and has trouble telling from his alignment. That flexibility is the whole
value: one player who can be a safety, a slot corner and a linebacker lets the defense change
its shape without changing its personnel, which means the offense can't use substitutions to
force a mismatch. It has made him a first-team All-Pro twice, for 2023 and 2025.[^hamiltonap]

**What to notice:** before the snap, where is 14, and does he move? If he starts deep and
creeps down late, something is coming. If he starts in the box and races back to the deep
middle at the snap, the defense just changed its
[**coverage shell**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-shell-coverage-shell) (how many
safeties play deep) on you. You'll learn to name those moves in
[Disguise, Rotation, and Split-Field Coverage](../06-pass-coverage/06-06-disguise-rotation-and-split-field.qmd).
:::

A lead run ('iso') from the I-formation against a base 4-3, in seconds after the snap; the running back (R) is ringed and carries the ball. The left tackle drives the defensive end outward; the left guard and center double-team the tackle shaded over the center, and then the center comes off the double-team onto the Mike. That opens a hole between the left guard and left tackle. The fullback (F) leads through it and meets the Will in the hole, the tight end blocks the Sam on the far side, and the receivers block the cornerbacks out wide (off this zoomed view). The offense can block nine defenders at most, so two go unblocked: the safeties, the farthest from the hole. The free safety, filling from the left, is the man the runner has to beat.
:::
:::


Go through it one position at a time, the way you'll learn to watch a replay:

- **Offensive line:** each lineman blocks the man in front of him, except that the left guard
  and center start by double-teaming the tackle over the center (a
  [**combo block**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-combo-block)), and then the center comes
  off it to block the Mike.
- **Quarterback:** opens, hands off, and (on a real play) carries out a fake so a defender
  has to think about him for half a second.
- **Fullback:** leads into the hole and blocks the first linebacker who shows (here, the
  Will). This one-on-one is the play's namesake: the fullback is "isolated" on the Will.
- **Tailback:** takes the handoff, stays a couple of yards behind the fullback, and cuts off
  his block.
- **Tight end and receivers:** block. The tight end takes the Sam on the far side, and the
  receivers' blocks on the cornerbacks are what turn a five-yard gain into a long one if the
  runner breaks a tackle.
- **Defensive linemen:** take on their blockers and try not to get moved.
- **Linebackers:** read the run and fill. The Will takes on the fullback; the Mike is picked
  up by the center coming off the double-team; the Sam is blocked by the tight end.
- **Safeties:** the two players nobody blocks. The free safety reads run and fills the alley
  (the lane between the blocks and the sideline), and he's the man the tailback has to beat.
- **Cornerbacks:** play their receivers until they're sure it's a run.

Now count. The quarterback and the ball carrier don't block, so the offense has **nine
blockers for eleven defenders**: two defenders always go unblocked, and the offense's only
choice is *which* two. The usual answer is the two farthest from the hole, here the safeties,
because by the time they arrive the runner should be five yards downfield at full speed
(coaches call that "blocked to the safety"). The last frame shows exactly that: the play has
gained its yards, and whether it gains more depends on one tackle in space. Which defenders
the offense leaves alone, and how it makes them wrong, runs through the whole run game
([The Language of the Run Game](../03-the-run-game/03-01-run-game-language.qmd)), sets up the
box count, and becomes [Option Football](../03-the-run-game/03-04-option-football.qmd), where
the offense *reads* an unblocked defender instead of blocking him.

::: {.callout-tip title="Watch for it on Sunday: the one-player game"}
For one full drive, **watch only the center.** Ignore the ball. On every snap, say out loud
what he did:

- **Before the snap:** does he point at a defender or shout something? (He's naming the
  defender the blocking scheme counts from.) Does the quarterback point first and the center
  echo him, or the other way round?
- **At the snap:** under center or shotgun? A shotgun snap is a five-yard toss; watch whether
  the center's head comes up fast.
- **After the snap:** did he block the man over him, help a guard with a double-team, climb
  to a linebacker, or (on a screen pass, a short throw to a receiver or back with blockers set
  up in front of him) release downfield to block in space? Did he ever touch the ball again?
  (He shouldn't.)

Then, if you have time for more:

- **Count the defensive backs** on first-and-10. Four means a base defense; five means
  nickel, usually a slot corner and sometimes a third safety. The safeties are often off the
  top of your screen before the snap, so you may have to count them on the replay
  ([How to Watch a Broadcast](01-06-how-to-watch-a-broadcast.qmd) shows where to look).
- **Find the tight end before the snap** and predict which side the Sam linebacker and the
  strong safety will line up on. Most teams set to him; some set to the wide side of the
  field instead, and spotting which one a defense does is a real scouting clue.
- **On a punt, find the gunners** before the snap and count how many defenders the return
  team puts on each: one or two?
- **Check a jersey.** When a player in the 50s–70s lines up somewhere unusual (out at tight
  end, in the backfield), listen for the referee's announcement that he's reporting as
  eligible.
:::

**Which of 1, 2 and 3 is the Mike, the Sam and the Will? Which of 4 and 5 is the strong
safety? And which side of the field would you expect a defensive coordinator to worry about
for the run?**

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}
**1 is the Sam, 2 is the Mike, 3 is the Will; 4 is the strong safety.** The names come from
the tight end. He's on the offense's left (your left as you look at the picture), so that's
the strong side: the Sam (1) lines up there, across from the tight end, ready to take on his
block, and the strong safety (4) sits on that side, a little closer to the line than the free
safety. The Mike (2) is in the middle, and the Will (3) is on the weak side, away from the
tight end, where there are fewer blockers.

**The run worry is the strong side.** The tight end gives the offense an extra blocker on the
left, so more gaps to fill there; that's exactly why the defense puts its biggest
linebacker and its run-support safety on that side. The obvious follow-up: then why doesn't
the offense just run the other way, at the lighter weak side? It does, often, and that's why
the Will has to be the fastest linebacker on the field: the weak side is light by design, and
he's the one who has to cover the ground. If the tight end flipped to the right before the
snap, all of those names would flip with him. Watching the Sam move when the tight end moves
is one of the first live "reads" you can make.
:::
:::

**How many defensive linemen, linebackers and defensive backs are on the field? What does
that tell you about what the defense expects, and which defensive players have left the
field compared with the base defense?**

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}
**Four linemen, one linebacker, six defensive backs.** The four squares on the line are the
defensive linemen. Only one defender stands in the middle at linebacker depth, inside the
box. The other six are defensive backs, and each is lined up on a receiver or deep: a
cornerback on each outside receiver, one defender over each of the two inside receivers on
the right, and two safeties deep.

Six defensive backs is called **dime** (two nickels, so to speak), a package taught in
[A First Look at Defense](../02-personnel-and-formations/02-05-a-first-look-at-defense.qmd).
Compared with the base 4-3, **two linebackers have left**, almost certainly the Sam and one of
the others, replaced by two extra defensive backs. The linebacker who stays is usually the
best cover linebacker, often the Mike or the Will. The defense is telling you it expects a
pass: on third-and-9 the offense needs nine yards, a run rarely gets that, and the defense
wants as many fast cover players on the field as it can afford.

A caution: the sixth defensive back doesn't always stand out wide. Many teams put him at
linebacker depth inside the box as a "dime backer," and then you'd spot him by his size and
number (a 200-pounder in the 20s or 30s), not by where he stands. And the price of dime is
that only five defenders (four linemen and one linebacker) are near the ball, so a
[**draw**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-draw) (a run disguised as a pass, with the
quarterback dropping back before he hands off) or a quarterback run is the offense's natural
counter, and you'll see it on third-and-long more than you'd expect.
:::
:::

**Which players may catch a forward pass on this play? The tight end, 87, catches one
ten yards downfield. Will there be a flag?**

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}
**Eligible: 11, 13, 84, 23 and the quarterback, 9. Not eligible: the five linemen and the
tight end, 87. Yes, a flag.**

Count the line. Eight players are on it: 11, the five linemen, 87 and 13. (Eight is legal;
the rule is *at least* seven.) Only the two ends of that line are eligible, and the ends are
11 on the left and **13 on the right**, because 13 is lined up on the line *outside* the tight
end. That "covers" 87: he's on the line but not at the end of it, so on this play he's an
ineligible receiver despite being a tight end with an eligible number. The officials will
throw a flag: an ineligible player may not catch a forward pass (and, ten yards downfield, he
was also well past the one yard an ineligible player is allowed). The penalties themselves
are in [Contact Rules and Penalties](../09-special-teams-and-the-rules-that-shape-strategy/09-03-contact-rules-and-penalties.qmd);
the catch itself is *illegal touching of a forward pass*, a 5-yard foul.[^illegaltouch]

The backs are 84 (a yard off the line), 23, and the quarterback. **The quarterback is
eligible here**, because he's in the shotgun rather than taking a hand-to-hand snap under
center, so he counts as a back, exactly as Nick Foles did on the Philly Special.

This is why the rules care so much about a one-yard step. Move 13 off the line, and 87
becomes the end and eligible again. Offenses use exactly this kind of adjustment to change
who's eligible, and the defense has to notice. More in
[Formation Rules and the Language of Alignment](../02-personnel-and-formations/02-02-formation-rules-and-vocabulary.qmd).
:::
:::

## Takeaways

- Football has **three teams on one roster**: offense, defense, special teams. Unlimited
  substitution (permanent in the NFL since 1950) let each player specialize, which is why
  bodies now match jobs so closely.
- **Offense:** five **linemen** (center, guards, tackles) who block and may not catch passes;
  a **quarterback**; one or two **backs** (running back, sometimes a fullback); and
  pass-catchers split between **wide receivers** (X, Z, slot) and the **tight end**, who is
  half blocker and half receiver, and whose side names the strong side.
- **Eligibility is a rule about alignment:** seven on the line, and only the two ends and the
  backs (anyone off the line) may catch a pass, never a quarterback under center. Jersey
  numbers 50–79 mark the ineligible linemen.
- **Defense:** a **front seven** of linemen (tackles, nose, ends/**edge rushers**) and
  linebackers (**Mike**, **Sam** on the tight end side, **Will** away from it), and a
  **secondary** of cornerbacks, safeties and, in the modern default, a **slot cornerback**.
  The closer a defender stands to the ball, the more he's built for the run.
- **Special teams** have their own specialists: kicker, punter, long snapper, holder,
  returner, gunner.
- **Position, alignment, assignment** are three different things: who he is, where he
  stands, what he does. Reading the game means using alignment to guess assignment, and the
  best players (and coaches) blur the three on purpose.
